extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers studying federalism and constitutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and assess the institutional features, preconditions, and consequences that make a federal constitution effective or defective, with emphasis on the U.S. example and comparative lessons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of legislators (intelligence and patriotism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislators should be chosen for intelligence and patriotism and be willing to propose restrictions and withstand popular passions when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text emphasizes that founders were 'distinguished as almost all the legislators of the Union were for their intelligence, they were still more so for their patriotism.' Includes Hamilton's argument (Federalist No. 71) that guardians appointed by the people must 'withstand the temporary delusion' to save the public from fatal consequences; examples and praise for those who acted at peril of public displeasure. Anti-pattern: legislators who respond only to transient popular impulses or flatter prejudices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate term lengths for representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Design of term duration should balance responsiveness to constituents and freedom for representatives to exercise independent judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter notes state Houses often had one-year terms and Senates two, making members 'constantly and narrowly tied down by the slightest desires of their constituents'; the Federal Constitution increased durations to 'give them freer scope for the exercise of their own judgment.' Scoring note: very short terms = excessive dependence; longer, but not unchecked, terms = greater deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bicameral design that yields a deliberative upper house
rubrics_metrics.description: Two legislative branches should differ in eligibility and mode of election so one chamber represents a superior degree of intelligence and discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal design changed 'conditions of eligibility and the mode of election' to produce an upper house of mature age chosen by an elected assembly of limited members; purpose is to temper rapid representation of popular passions. Anti-pattern: bicameral bodies composed in the same way so both echo the same popular impulses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks against concentration of power in the legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitution must prevent the legislature from monopolizing all species of influence and social force, which would lead to despotism of the majority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville warns that concentrating social force in the legislature is 'prejudicial to a well-conducted administration, and favorable to the despotism of the majority.' Guidance: build independent executive and judiciary, varied term lengths, and other structural checks to resist democratic centralization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive independence and protective powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive should possess sufficient independence and tools (term stability, salary protection, staff, veto) to resist purely transient popular pressure and to execute national laws effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast between weak state executives (annually rotating, subject to salary changes, passive agents) and the Federal President: single individual, four-year term, salary cannot be altered during term, protected by official dependents, and armed with a suspensive veto. These features are recommended to confer 'a strong and independent position upon the executive authority within the limits prescribed to it.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence from legislative influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Judiciary must be separated and protected (unalterable salaries, inalienable functions, independent tenure) to prevent legislative domination of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In many states the legislature 'reserved to itself the right of regulating the emoluments of the judges' or appointed judges temporarily; by contrast the Federal Constitution 'provides for the independence of the judges, by declaring that their salary shall not be altered, and that their functions shall be inalienable.' Anti-pattern: legislative control of judge pay or temporary appointments that subject judges to legislative pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal government's direct authority and enforcement capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful federal government must be able to execute its own laws directly on individuals (levy taxes on inhabitants, maintain its own army and courts) rather than depend on constituent states for enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville contrasts earlier confederations that 'demanded its supplies at the hands of the separate Governments' and failed, with the U.S. Union which 'rules individuals: the national Government levies a tax... upon each inhabitant,' and is 'served by its own civil and military officers, by its own army, and its own courts of justice.' Scoring: capacity for direct enforcement = essential for effective federal authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of the division of sovereignty / jurisdictional boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Spheres of authority between federal and state governments must be accurately defined so collisions are minimized and citizens can discern obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The federal system 'rests upon a theory which is necessarily complicated' and requires limiting each sovereignty to an 'accurately defined' sphere. If boundaries are obscure, 'numberless difficulties remain to be solved' and collisions occur (Mexican example). Practical implication: legislation and institutions should make jurisdictional lines intelligible to judges and citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizen political competence and practical judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal systems demand a high level of practical political knowledge among ordinary citizens, who must daily exercise discretion and distinguish federal from state obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville praises Americans' ability to 'distinguish, with surprising facility, the obligations created by the laws of Congress from those created by the laws of his own State' and to point out limits of jurisdictions. Anti-pattern: societies where political science has not 'descended to the humblest classes' will struggle with federal complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural preconditions for federalism (social/geographic/cultural bonds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful federalism requires underlying natural causes of union—shared origin, manners, opinions, and sufficient mutual interest—without which federal constitutions copied in form will fail in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville argues Mexico copied the American Constitution but lacked the 'spirit and the sense' to make it work, leading to collisions and anarchy or military rule. He notes that widely separated parts (Maine and Georgia) can be naturally united if common causes exist, unlike unrelated provinces (Normandy and Brittany). Evaluation should weigh cultural and social readiness, not only institutional text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing local autonomy with national strength
rubrics_metrics.description: A federal arrangement should combine the advantages of small nations (local responsiveness, active improvement, civic habit) with those of great nations (military strength, broad commerce, intellectual centers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal system 'was created with the intention of combining the different advantages which result from the greater and the lesser extent of nations.' In practice this means reserving details to provincial legislatures while Congress handles principal national measures; benefits include local experiments and national capacity in foreign affairs and defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of inherent relative weakness of divided sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: Designs must acknowledge that divided sovereignty is inherently weaker than unitary supremacy and incorporate remedies to mitigate this relative weakness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville calls the 'relative weakness of the government of the Union' the second and most fatal defect inherent in federal systems. He notes the partition of sovereignty 'must always be less powerful than an entire supremacy' and that Americans mitigated but did not eliminate this danger. Practical evaluation should assess how institutional features compensate for this weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complexity as a systemic cost and need for simplification
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal systems are complex and demand intellectual resources from citizens and legislators; simplicity of principle aids political durability while complexity requires ongoing civic prudence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter observes that 'two sovereignties are necessarily in presence of each other' and that complexity 'demands the daily exercise of a considerable share of discretion.' It warns that parties often adopt single, simple symbols to act, so institutional design should seek to simplify choices where possible to avoid paralysis or demagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: External threat profile suitability (war and security considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The desirability of the federal model depends on external security conditions—federalism is less suitable for peoples frequently exposed to great wars or external aggression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville states 'War, the main peril of confederations' and argues the U.S. had no great wars to fear at the time, which made federalism practicable; by contrast in Europe or in states with frequent external threats federal arrangements may fail. Evaluation should factor in strategic/geopolitical context.
